title: File Uploads & Supabase Storage
readme:
Phase 27 - File Uploads and Supabase Storage

This package completes Volume 07. It teaches a private signed-upload-intent architecture in which NestJS authorizes Task attachment operations, Supabase Storage stores bytes, and PostgreSQL stores TaskAttachment metadata.

Files are intentionally split into focused books plus a combined edition. See reference/TaskFlow_Storage_Snapshot for implementation examples.

lessons.body:
Storage Mental Model: Public, Private
and Source of Truth
TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026

Storage is object storage, not a relational domain model
Two systems, different responsibilities

Supabase Storage                                 TaskFlow PostgreSQL
objectPath
object bytes                                   which Task owns it

object path                                     who uploaded it

object metadata                                display name/type/size

signed access                                    workflow status

Do not use storage.objects as your business-domain attachment table.

Public vs private
• Public bucket: anyone with the object URL can fetch the object; useful for genuinely public assets.

• Private bucket: reads require authenticated authorization or a signed URL. Task attachments are
private by default.

Do not edit storage.objects directly
Supabase stores Storage metadata in Postgres, but its documentation explicitly recommends treating
the storage schema as read-only and performing object mutations through Storage APIs. Deleting
metadata with SQL does not reliably delete the underlying object.

TaskFlow decision
PostgreSQL owns TaskAttachment rows and relationships. Supabase Storage owns bytes. objectPath is
the bridge between them.

lessons.body:
Signed Upload Intent Architecture
TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026

Why not proxy every byte through NestJS
A backend proxy can work, but it makes the API server carry file bandwidth, memory and timeout
pressure. TaskFlow instead lets the browser upload directly to Storage after NestJS authorizes a
narrowly scoped upload intent.

End-to-end flow

TaskFlow attachment upload - authorization stays in NestJS

Browser                      NestJS                            Postgres                 Storage            Browser
file                   upload intent                       PENDING row             signed token       direct upload

NestJS finalize                                 Postgres
verify object                              READY metadata

Storage holds bytes. PostgreSQL holds application meaning and relationships.

Trust boundary
Signed upload intent - trust boundary

Browser                                NestJS                         Signed token               Storage

untrusted filename                  auth + permission                     one object path          enforces bucket

MIME + size                         allowlist + limit                   time limited             constraints

service-role key remains server-only

original filename is metadata - not the authoritative object path

Two-step commit
• Intent endpoint validates Task access, file policy and requested metadata, creates a PENDING row,
then returns a signed upload token.

• Browser transfers bytes directly to the exact object path.

• Finalize endpoint checks the object exists and its Storage metadata matches the expected size/type,
then marks the row READY.

Why PENDING matters
Direct object storage and PostgreSQL are separate systems. A PENDING state gives
TaskFlow an explicit way to represent “intent exists but upload is not yet committed to the
application”.

lessons.body:
Attachment Data Model and Prisma
Migration
TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026

Domain model
enum AttachmentStatus {
PENDING
READY
DELETING
}

model TaskAttachment {
id           String           @id @default(uuid())
taskId       String
uploadedById String
bucket       String           @default("task-attachments")
objectPath   String           @unique
originalName String
mimeType     String
sizeBytes    Int
status       AttachmentStatus @default(PENDING)
createdAt    DateTime         @default(now())
readyAt      DateTime?

task       Task @relation(fields: [taskId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
uploadedBy User @relation(fields: [uploadedById], references: [id], onDelete: Restrict)

@@index([taskId, status, createdAt])
@@index([uploadedById])
}

Why metadata belongs here
• Task ownership and authorization need relational joins.

• Original display filename must survive even though the object path is randomized.

• PENDING/READY/DELETING are application workflow states, not Storage object states.

• Audit/reporting can reference uploader, Task and timestamps without scanning a bucket.

Migration note
Add the model and Task/User relations using the same Prisma 7.9.1 migration workflow from Phase 09.
Do not hand-edit the Storage schema.

lessons.body:
Private Bucket Configuration and
Server Storage Client
TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026

Bucket policy
await supabase.storage.createBucket(
"task-attachments",
{
public: false,
allowedMimeTypes: [
"application/pdf",
"image/png",
"image/jpeg",
"text/plain",
],
fileSizeLimit: "20MB",
},
)

Why both application validation and bucket limits
NestJS validation gives business-friendly errors and authorization. Bucket limits provide a second
enforcement layer if a client tries to upload bytes that violate the configured size or MIME constraints.

Server-only client
const storageAdmin = createClient(
config.getOrThrow("SUPABASE_URL"),
config.getOrThrow("SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY"),
{
auth: {
persistSession: false,
autoRefreshToken: false,
},
},
)

Critical secret rule
SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY bypasses Storage RLS and must never be exposed through
NEXT_PUBLIC_*, browser bundles, logs, or error payloads. NestJS must perform authorization before
using this client.

Why TaskFlow does not need broad browser Storage RLS
The browser receives a signed token for one pre-authorized object path. This keeps the primary
business authorization policy in NestJS instead of duplicating Task membership rules across Storage
RLS.

lessons.summary: File Policy, Safe Object Paths and Validation TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026 Client metadata is untrusted • file.name may contain awkward characters or misleading extensions. • file.type is supplied by the client and can be spoofed. • Size can be checked client-side for UX…
lessons.body:
File Policy, Safe Object Paths and
Validation
TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026

Client metadata is untrusted
• file.name may contain awkward characters or misleading extensions.

• file.type is supplied by the client and can be spoofed.

• Size can be checked client-side for UX but must be enforced again server-side and by the bucket.

Allowlist schema
const allowedMimeTypes = z.enum([
"application/pdf",
"image/png",
"image/jpeg",
"text/plain",
])

export const createAttachmentIntentSchema = z.object({
originalName: z.string().trim().min(1).max(255),
mimeType: allowedMimeTypes,
sizeBytes: z.number().int().positive()
.max(20 * 1024 * 1024),
})

Do not use original filename as identity
const extensionByMime = {
"application/pdf": "pdf",
"image/png": "png",
"image/jpeg": "jpg",
"text/plain": "txt",
} as const

const objectPath =
`workspaces/${workspaceId}` +
`/tasks/${taskId}` +
`/${attachmentId}.${extensionByMime[mimeType]}`

Security consequence
The object path is generated from trusted identifiers and an allowlisted extension. The original filename
is stored only as display metadata, eliminating path traversal and collision pressure from user-supplied
names.

High-risk file types
For executables, macro-enabled Office files, archives or regulated uploads, MIME allowlists are not
enough. A stronger design adds quarantine plus malware/content scanning before READY.

lessons.body:
Resumable TUS Uploads and Progress
TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026

When TaskFlow switches to TUS
• File is larger than 6MB.

• Users frequently upload over unstable networks.

• Product requires progress and resumability.

Dependency
pnpm --filter web add tus-js-client@4.3.1

Signed TUS upload sketch
const upload = new tus.Upload(file, {
endpoint:
`https://${projectRef}.storage.supabase.co` +
`/storage/v1/upload/resumable`,

headers: {
"x-signature": signedUploadToken,
},

metadata: {
bucketName: "task-attachments",
objectName: objectPath,
contentType: file.type,
},

chunkSize: 6 * 1024 * 1024,
retryDelays: [0, 3000, 5000, 10000, 20000],
removeFingerprintOnSuccess: true,

onProgress(bytesUploaded, bytesTotal) {
onProgress(bytesUploaded / bytesTotal)
},

onSuccess() {
void completeAttachment(attachmentId)
},
})

upload.start()

Important implementation details
• Use the direct project-ref.storage.supabase.co hostname for large uploads.

• Supabase currently requires 6MB TUS chunks.

• Signed upload tokens can be forwarded in the x-signature header.

• Progress is a transfer-progress signal; the attachment is not READY until NestJS finalizes it.

Course default
Keep standard signed upload as the simplest path for small files. Add TUS only when file size or UX
requirements justify the extra moving parts.

Private Downloads and Short-Lived
Signed URLs
TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026

Download authorization
A browser should not receive a permanent public object URL for Task documents. It first asks NestJS for
access to an attachment. NestJS verifies Task visibility using the same Workspace authorization rules
from Phase 19.

Signed download
const { data, error } = await storage
.from(attachment.bucket)
.createSignedUrl(
attachment.objectPath,
60,
{ download: true },
)

if (error) throw error
return {
url: data.signedUrl,
expiresIn: 60,
}

Why short-lived URLs
• The URL can be handed to the browser without exposing the service-role key.

• Access naturally expires.

• The application can re-check authorization every time it issues a new URL.

Do not put signed URLs in durable state
A signed URL is a temporary capability. Store bucket + objectPath in PostgreSQL, then mint
a fresh URL when needed.

lessons.body:
Replacement, Deletion and Orphan
Cleanup
TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026

Replacement strategy
Do not overwrite the same object path by default. Upload a new UUID-named object, verify it, update
the application metadata/reference, then clean up the old object. This avoids stale-caching behavior
and gives rollback options.

Deletion is a distributed workflow
Deletion across database + object storage is not one ACID transaction

READY                     DELETING           Storage.remove              DB delete
metadata                    mark row             delete bytes             remove row

If a step fails, keep enough state to retry cleanup safely.

Recommended delete flow
• Authorize attachment deletion in NestJS.

• Mark metadata DELETING so concurrent UI actions stop treating it as normal.

• Call storage.remove([objectPath]).

• After successful object deletion, remove the TaskAttachment row.

• If Storage deletion fails, retain DELETING (or restore READY) and retry operationally.

Orphan cleanup
• PENDING rows older than the signed-upload lifetime may indicate abandoned intents.

• Cleanup job checks whether an object exists; remove any abandoned bytes and delete stale
metadata.

• Object without TaskAttachment metadata is an orphan and still consumes storage.

• Do not delete directly from storage.objects; use the Storage API.

Why this is not one database transaction
PostgreSQL and object storage cannot share the same local Prisma transaction. Correctness comes
from explicit workflow states, idempotent operations and compensating cleanup.

Testing, Security, Troubleshooting and
Phase Exit
TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026

Security test matrix
• Unauthenticated intent request -> 401.

• Authenticated non-member attaches to another Workspace Task -> 404/403 according to policy.

• Disallowed MIME or >20MB -> rejected before signed token issuance.

• Path sent by browser is ignored; server generates objectPath.

• Service-role key never appears in web bundle or API response.

• Finalize without an object -> failure; row remains non-READY.

• Finalize with size/type mismatch -> failure.

• Download for unauthorized caller -> denied.

• Expired signed download -> no permanent access.

• Delete failure leaves recoverable state for retry.

Common failures
• 400 Asset Already Exists: path collision or unintended reuse; unique UUID paths avoid this.

• 413/size error: global or bucket limits are lower than the application policy.

• TUS stalls/retries: verify direct storage hostname, 6MB chunks, token header and network
conditions.

• Signed upload works but finalize fails: inspect info() result and expected metadata.

• Object remains after business deletion: run orphan/deletion retry workflow; do not manipulate
storage tables directly.

Phase exit checklist
• Private bucket configured with allowed MIME types and 20MB limit.

• TaskAttachment migration applied.

• Signed upload intent is authorized by NestJS.

• Small-file upload works; TUS path understood/tested if enabled.

• Finalize verifies object metadata and marks READY.

• Download uses short-lived signed URL.

• Delete/replacement have explicit failure recovery.

• Tests prove cross-Workspace file access is denied.

Debugging Workshop — Phase 27: File Uploads & Supabase Storage

Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.

The debugging loop
1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action.
2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state.
3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior.
4. Form one hypothesis.
5. Change one variable.
6. Re-run the same reproduction.
7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis.

Boundary walk
upload intent -> API authorization/validation -> signed upload or storage request -> object store -> finalize metadata -> signed/read access

Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next.

Failure drill 1 — Trusting filename extension as MIME proof

Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — File Uploads & Supabase Storage

Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 27 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?

Required outcome
Design a secure file-upload pipeline with storage objects, metadata, validation, signed access, lifecycle cleanup, and authorization.

Required artifact
Task attachment upload/download/delete workflow using Supabase Storage plus application metadata.

Constraints
• Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch.
• Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt.
• Keep changes scoped to the capability.
• Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases.
• Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable.

Acceptance criteria
• Can separate object bytes and metadata.
• Can validate/authorize upload intent.
• Can use signed access.
• Can reason about partial failure cleanup.

Independent build sequence
1. Define file policy: allowed types, size, naming/path rules, ownership, retention.
2. Create an upload-intent endpoint that checks authenticated user and target task access before granting upload capability.
3. Upload bytes directly to storage where appropriate rather than proxying large files through the API by default.
4. Finalize by verifying object existence and committing metadata transactionally as far as the architecture allows.
5. Generate time-limited access for private objects and test outsider access denial.
6. Implement delete/cleanup behavior for abandoned uploads and metadata/object mismatch.

Self-review
Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence.

Stretch challenge
Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Predict whether your design still behaves correctly. If not, document the next architectural improvement rather than adding complexity blindly.

Phase exit
Run the relevant checks, inspect Git diff, and write a three-sentence summary: what the system can do now, which boundary owns the new responsibility, and which failure you now know how to diagnose. Only then mark the phase complete.

# Attachment security checklist

- Private bucket by default.
- Service-role key only in NestJS/server environment.
- NestJS authorizes Task membership before issuing upload/download capabilities.
- Server generates object paths; never trust client-supplied paths.
- Allowlist MIME types and cap size in API + bucket.
- Original name is display metadata only.
- Finalize verifies object existence, size and content type.
- Signed download URLs are short-lived.
- Do not store signed URLs in PostgreSQL.
- Do not mutate `storage.objects` directly.
- Add malware/quarantine scanning for higher-risk file classes.
- Clean abandoned PENDING uploads and failed DELETING records.

# TaskFlow Phase 27 - File Uploads and Supabase Storage

Reference snapshot for a signed-upload-intent architecture. NestJS authorizes attachment operations, Supabase Storage holds bytes, and PostgreSQL stores application metadata.

Default bucket: `task-attachments` (private). Default app limit: 20 MB.

- Supabase Storage overview: https://supabase.com/docs/guides/storage
- Supabase Standard Uploads: https://supabase.com/docs/guides/storage/uploads/standard-uploads
- Supabase Resumable Uploads: https://supabase.com/docs/guides/storage/uploads/resumable-uploads
- Supabase Storage Access Control: https://supabase.com/docs/guides/storage/security/access-control
- Supabase Storage Ownership: https://supabase.com/docs/guides/storage/security/ownership
- Supabase Storage Schema: https://supabase.com/docs/guides/storage/schema/design
- Supabase File Limits: https://supabase.com/docs/guides/storage/uploads/file-limits
- Supabase createSignedUploadUrl: https://supabase.com/docs/reference/javascript/file-buckets-createsigneduploadurl
- Supabase uploadToSignedUrl: https://supabase.com/docs/reference/javascript/file-buckets-uploadtosignedurl
- Supabase createSignedUrl: https://supabase.com/docs/reference/javascript/file-buckets-createsignedurl
- Supabase info: https://supabase.com/docs/reference/javascript/file-buckets-info
- Supabase createBucket: https://supabase.com/docs/reference/javascript/file-buckets-createbucket
- tus-js-client npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/tus-js-client

enum AttachmentStatus {
  PENDING
  READY
  DELETING
}

model TaskAttachment {
  id           String           @id @default(uuid())
  taskId       String
  uploadedById String
  bucket       String           @default("task-attachments")
  objectPath   String           @unique
  originalName String
  mimeType     String
  sizeBytes    Int
  status       AttachmentStatus @default(PENDING)
  createdAt    DateTime         @default(now())
  readyAt      DateTime?

  task       Task @relation(fields: [taskId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)

export const ATTACHMENT_BUCKET = "task-attachments"
export const MAX_ATTACHMENT_BYTES = 20 * 1024 * 1024

export const ALLOWED_ATTACHMENT_MIME_TYPES = [
  "application/pdf",
  "image/png",
  "image/jpeg",
  "text/plain",
] as const

export const ATTACHMENT_EXTENSION_BY_MIME = {
  "application/pdf": "pdf",
  "image/png": "png",
  "image/jpeg": "jpg",
  "text/plain": "txt",
} as const

import { z } from "zod"
import { ALLOWED_ATTACHMENT_MIME_TYPES, MAX_ATTACHMENT_BYTES } from "./attachment.constants"

export const createAttachmentIntentSchema = z.strictObject({
  originalName: z.string().trim().min(1).max(255),
  mimeType: z.enum(ALLOWED_ATTACHMENT_MIME_TYPES),
  sizeBytes: z.number().int().positive().max(MAX_ATTACHMENT_BYTES),
})

export type CreateAttachmentIntent = z.infer<typeof createAttachmentIntentSchema>

# Phase 27 test matrix

## Authorization
- No token cannot create an upload intent.
- Member outside the Task Workspace cannot attach/download/delete.
- Valid member can create an intent for an authorized Task.

## Validation
- Zero-byte, >20MB and disallowed MIME are rejected.
- Client cannot choose an object path.
- Generated paths are unique and Workspace/Task scoped.

## Lifecycle
- Intent creates PENDING metadata.
- Successful upload + matching Storage info becomes READY.
- Missing object cannot finalize.
- Metadata mismatch cannot finalize.
- Signed download expires.
- Delete removes bytes then metadata or leaves a recoverable DELETING state.
- Stale PENDING intents are cleaned.
